subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Who is the author of Animal Farm?
questions.explain: Animal Farm was written by George Orwell, the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair.

questions.q: In which year was Animal Farm first published?
questions.explain: Orwell's novella was published in 1945, shortly before the end of the Second World War.

questions.q: Whose speech and vision of 'Animalism' first inspires the animals to rebel?
questions.explain: The prize boar Old Major delivers the speech that inspires the rebellion before dying.

questions.q: What is Boxer's personal maxim throughout the novel?
questions.explain: The loyal cart-horse Boxer repeatedly resolves 'I will work harder', showing his devotion.

questions.q: What is the farm called before the animals' rebellion?
questions.explain: The farm is Manor Farm under Mr Jones, renamed 'Animal Farm' after the rebellion.

questions.q: Which pig is chiefly responsible for spreading propaganda and persuading the other animals?
questions.explain: Squealer is the persuasive pig who manipulates the animals through propaganda and false statistics.

questions.q: Which single commandment eventually replaces all Seven Commandments on the barn wall?
options: 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others'
'Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy'
questions.explain: The Seven Commandments are reduced to this hypocritical maxim that justifies the pigs' privileges.

questions.q: Animal Farm is primarily an allegory of which historical event?
questions.explain: The novella is an allegory of the 1917 Russian Revolution and the rise of Stalinism.

questions.q: Which historical figure does the pig Napoleon most closely represent?
questions.explain: Napoleon, who seizes total control, is an allegory for the dictator Joseph Stalin.

questions.q: Snowball, who is driven from the farm by Napoleon's dogs, represents which real figure?
questions.explain: Snowball parallels Leon Trotsky, the rival leader exiled by Stalin.

questions.q: What does the windmill most strongly symbolise in the novel?
options: The Soviet drive for industrialisation and modernisation
The religious promise of an afterlife
questions.explain: The windmill mirrors Stalin's Five-Year Plans and the push to industrialise the Soviet Union.

questions.q: Why does Squealer repeatedly alter the Seven Commandments during the novel?
options: To justify the pigs' growing privileges and disguise their betrayal of the ideals
To make the rules easier for the sheep to memorise
To protect the animals from Mr Jones's return
To honour Old Major's original wishes
questions.explain: Each alteration retrospectively legitimises the pigs' corruption while masking their hypocrisy.

questions.q: What does the character of Boxer chiefly represent in the allegory?
options: The exploited and loyal working class
questions.explain: Boxer embodies the hardworking proletariat, exploited and ultimately betrayed by the leadership.

questions.q: The fierce dogs that Napoleon rears in secret are most likely a symbol of what?
questions.explain: The dogs represent the state's secret police, used to enforce Napoleon's power through terror.

questions.q: The slogan 'Four legs good, two legs bad', chanted by the sheep, best illustrates which idea?
options: How propaganda uses simple slogans to control thought
questions.explain: The reductive chant shows propaganda silencing dissent by replacing reasoned debate with slogans.

questions.q: The novel's cyclical structure, ending with the pigs resembling the humans they overthrew, most clearly suggests what?
options: That the revolution has been betrayed and power corrupts
That the animals were wrong to rebel at all
That humans and animals can live in harmony
That the windmill will finally succeed
questions.explain: The circular ending emphasises Orwell's warning that revolutionary ideals are corrupted by those who gain power.

questions.q: A student is writing an essay on how language is used to manipulate the truth. Which character offers the strongest evidence?
options: Squealer, who twists facts and rewrites the commandments
Benjamin, who refuses to speak out
Mollie, who cares only for ribbons
Mr Jones, who neglects the farm
questions.explain: Squealer's manipulation of language and statistics makes him the clearest example of propaganda in action.

questions.q: In tracing the plot's turning points, which moment marks the pigs' seizure of sole, unchallenged power?
options: Napoleon uses the dogs to chase Snowball from the farm
The animals win the Battle of the Cowshed
Old Major delivers his speech in the barn
questions.explain: Driving out Snowball removes Napoleon's only rival, marking the shift to one-pig dictatorship.

questions.q: To illustrate the theme that absolute power corrupts, which detail from the ending would be most effective to quote?
options: The pigs walking upright on two legs and carrying whips
Boxer being taken away in the van
The building of the first windmill
questions.explain: The pigs adopting human posture and tools shows their complete moral corruption into the tyrants they replaced.

questions.q: A student is building a revision table matching characters to their historical parallels. Which pairing is correct?
options: Old Major represents Karl Marx and revolutionary theory
Napoleon represents the Russian Orthodox Church
questions.explain: Old Major, whose ideas inspire the rebellion, parallels Karl Marx as the source of revolutionary ideology.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) English Literature (J352) specification; Animal Farm
